newsitem.title: USA: S&P says Mexico must build sustained growth.
newsitem.headline: S&P says Mexico must build sustained growth.

text.p: Standard and Poor's said Thursday that Mexico would need to address key long-term issues improve its credit rating, restore domestic confidence and build sustained economic growth.
"We see Mexico sitting quite appropriately in the BB category," which is speculative grade, said Lacey Gallagher, S&P director of sovereign ratings on a conference call.
S&P raised its outlook on Mexico's BB foreign currency obligations to stable from negative on Tuesday, but said Mexico would probably not reach investment grade in the medium term.

Gallagher said "a better sustainable rate of GDP growth, maintaining the orthodox fiscal program that has been in effect, continuing monetary policy directed toward disinflation and improving the banking sector ... are some things we will be looking at for the medium term,"
Gallagher said S&P would also be watching Mexico's transformation to a more open political system, but political factors have had a "minimal impact" on economic policy.
"Liberalization is proceeding very gradually, as a result we don't expect it to influence economic policy," Gallagher said.
"Broader popular support is not proving necessary for economic policy continuity," Gallagher said.

Last week's rebel strikes in southern and eastern Mexico also seemed unlikely to challenge the countries credit standing, as Gallagher said she expected the government to manage such activity over time, if the group persists.

On the macro-economic side, the government should be able to maintain a fiscal deficit less that 1.0 percent of GDP next year, Gallagher said. "We expect the government to maintain its commitmment to sound public finances."

Critical for the country would be the expansion of domestic savings to reduce reliance on foreign capital, S&P said. "The challenge will be to maintain stablity and implement the private pension system in order to improve domestic savings," Gallagher said.
The country would also benefit greatly from a strengthened bank sector, and has the resources to solve the banking problems without a direct impact on the system, S&P said.
"It's recovery and development into a stronger, more efficient, market-oriented financial system will take 3-5 years," said S&P Analyst Victor Herrera.
